title: Keep your half of the tally
word: Keep your half of the tally
hook: after a great quarrel, some resentment stays; the sage keeps his side of the tally and demands nothing (Tao Te Ching 79)

segments.voice: Yesterday, nothing softer than water: the softest thing wears down the hard by never stopping. Your line was water wins. Did you do your small thing, and plan it again? Day one thousand one hundred forty-one.

The fight is over. Apologies were said, maybe even hugs. Everyone agreed to move on. And yet, a month later, a small remark lands wrong, and there it is again: the old sting, right where it was. Making peace and being at peace turn out to be two different things. Chapter seventy-nine of the Tao Te Ching starts exactly there, with what's left over after the peace treaty is signed.
screen: `THE FIGHT IS OVER.` → `THE STING IS STILL THERE.` → `WHAT'S LEFT OVER.`

segments.voice: First, the leftover. When a great resentment is settled, the chapter says, some resentment is sure to remain. How can that be called good? It's a frank admission. Patching things up after a big break doesn't get everything back. Better, the chapter implies, not to pile up the debt in the first place. Second, the tally. A tally, as commentators describe it, is a record of an agreement split into two halves, one for each side, so the halves can be matched later. The chapter says the sage holds his half of the tally, and makes no demands on the other person. He has the proof. He just doesn't press it. Third, two kinds of people. Those with virtue, the chapter says, look after the tally; those without it look after collecting. One keeps the agreement and lets it rest. The other is always out knocking on doors for what's owed. Fourth, the last line. Heaven's way has no favorites, it says, and it is always with the good person. That is the week's thread pulled tight. Heaven's net is loose but loses nothing. Threats wound the one who holds them. Hunger traces back to those who take too much. Soft is alive. The bow lowers the high. Water wins by never forcing. And today: hold your half, and don't collect. On an ordinary Tuesday, this looks like knowing exactly what someone owes you, and choosing not to send the bill.
screen: `SOME RESENTMENT REMAINS.` · `THE SAGE HOLDS HIS HALF.` · `KEEP THE TALLY, DON'T COLLECT.` · `A WEEK OF NOT FORCING.` · then, large: `DEMAND NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: drop one demand. Sit and let the breath settle without asking anything of it. Then bring to mind one thing you've been waiting for someone to give you: an apology, a thank-you, a favor returned, money owed. You may well be right that it's owed. Hold your half of the tally, the knowledge of it, without needing to press it. Picture setting the demand down beside you, for these two minutes. Notice what the hands, the chest, the jaw do when you stop collecting. The bell holds the time.
Keep your half of the tally. Chapter seventy-nine: the sage holds his half of the agreement and makes no demands on the other. Today's word.
screen: `KEEP YOUR HALF OF THE TALLY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: demand nothing. Today, let one thing you're owed stay owed, and see how the day goes without collecting it. Day one thousand one hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter seventy-nine as advice on old grievances: settling a great resentment leaves some behind, so the sage keeps his side of an agreement and does not press others for what they owe.

fork.setup: you hold your half of the tally. the other side owes you. what does the sage in chapter seventy-nine do?
options: hold the tally and make no demands.
fork.reveal: the sage keeps his half and demands nothing. those with virtue look after the tally; those without it look after collecting.

original.note: Chinese: the left half of the tally, which the sage holds in chapter seventy-nine.

trapdoor: what you thought: keep your half of the tally is about bookkeeping.
what it means: you can know what's owed to you and still choose not to press it.
what a scholar hears: the sage holds 左契, the left half of a split tally; commentators debate whether the left was the creditor's side.

notes: Week-end day: looks back at days 1135–1140 (chapters 73–78).
Chapter 79 is paraphrased; the writer could not confirm Legge's exact wording.
The description of a tally (wood or bamboo split in two, one half for each party) is general background, not stated in chapter 79; a Keeper should confirm or cut it under the claims rule.
'Those without it look after collecting' renders 無德司徹; 徹 is read by some as a tax levy. Confirm the paraphrase.
Trapdoor: whether the left half (左契) belonged to the creditor is debated in commentary; confirm the wording.
Original 左契 (zuǒ qì) rendered 'TSWAW chee'. Confirm.
